C00.title: Modern history starts in 1500. Here, it starts 200 years later.
facts: The Alto São Francisco lookout has a cross from 1718, the year the camp became the Town of São José.
From the same spot you see the Serra de São José, where the gold came from.

C01.title: Columbus misses the continent
facts: 3 ships (Santa María, Pinta, Niña) and about 90 men.
Left Palos on Aug 3, 1492; reached the Bahamas on Oct 12.
Thought he was in Asia and called the natives “Indians”.
notes: The exact island of landfall is debated.

C02.title: The Treaty of Tordesillas
facts: Signed on June 7, 1494.
An imaginary line 370 leagues west of Cape Verde: west for Spain, east for Portugal.
By the line, only a strip of Brazil's coast was Portuguese.

C03.title: The Spaniard who got there first
facts: Vicente Yáñez Pinzón, former captain of Columbus's Niña, touched the Northeast coast in January 1500.
By the treaty that land belonged to Portugal, so Spain made no claim.
notes: The exact landing spot is debated.

C04.title: Cabral and the stop along the way
facts: 13 ships, about 1,500 men. Landed at Porto Seguro (Bahia).
Thought it was an island (“Island of Vera Cruz”).
Sent one ship back with Pero Vaz de Caminha's letter and sailed on to India.
Left 2 convicts behind; 2 cabin boys ran away and stayed.
notes: Whether the landing was chance or intentional is debated.

C05.title: Rio de Janeiro in January
facts: A 1501–1502 reconnaissance expedition, with Amerigo Vespucci.
Named places after the saint of the day: All Saints' Bay (Nov 1), Rio de Janeiro (Jan 1502).

C06.title: The first contract: brazilwood
facts: The tree gave a red dye valued for cloth in Europe; the name comes from “brasa”, ember.
The Crown leased the trade to merchant Fernão de Noronha (the island bears his name).
Indigenous people did the work in exchange for tools, mirrors and cloth: barter.

C07.title: The Cabo Frio trading post
facts: Feitoria = fortified warehouse to store brazilwood.
The oldest on record was near Cabo Frio (Rio), with about 24 men.

C08.title: The castaways who became chiefs
facts: Caramuru (Diogo Álvares) was shipwrecked in Bahia and married Paraguaçu, baptized in France in 1528 as Catarina.
João Ramalho lived among the Tupiniquim and married Bartira, daughter of chief Tibiriçá.
notes: Several details of these stories are debated.

C09.title: The castaway who reached the Incas
facts: Aleixo Garcia, a shipwreck survivor in Santa Catarina, crossed the continent on the Indigenous Peabiru trail.
The Peabiru was a network of Guarani paths about 3,000 km long.
He reached the Inca frontier and died on the way back.
notes: The exact route is debated.

C10.title: São Vicente, the first town
facts: Martim Afonso de Sousa founded São Vicente (São Paulo) on Jan 22, 1532: the first official town, with council and pillory.
One of the first sugar mills stood nearby (ruins of the Engenho dos Erasmos).

C11.title: The hereditary captaincies
facts: The coast was split into strips given to grantees who had to colonize at their own expense.
Almost all failed; Pernambuco (Duarte Coelho) and São Vicente worked, thanks to sugar.

C12.title: Salvador and the general government
facts: Tomé de Sousa founded Salvador, the first capital, in 1549.
He arrived with the first Jesuits (Manuel da Nóbrega).

C13.title: From “negros da terra” to Africans
facts: The first slavery was Indigenous (the so-called “negros da terra”).
With epidemics, resistance, Jesuit pressure and the profits of the Atlantic trade, African slavery grew.
Brazil received about 4.8 million enslaved Africans, close to 40% of the whole Atlantic trade.
notes: Figures are estimates from the SlaveVoyages database.

C14.title: Hans Staden almost becomes dinner
facts: Captured by the Tupinambá near Bertioga, he spent months awaiting ritual execution and managed to escape.
His book came out in 1557.

C15.title: The bishop who was eaten
facts: Pero Fernandes Sardinha was shipwrecked in Alagoas and killed by the Caeté.
In response, the Crown authorized the enslavement of the Caeté.

C16.title: The French in Rio and the Tamoio war
facts: Villegaignon founded France Antarctique in Guanabara Bay (1555).
The Tupinambá (Tamoio Confederation, with Cunhambebe and Aimberê) allied with the French.
Estácio de Sá founded Rio on March 1, 1565; the French left for good in 1567.
The Temiminó Arariboia, a Portuguese ally, founded Niterói.

C17.title: Anchieta and the poem in the sand
facts: José de Anchieta was held hostage by the Tamoio at Iperoig (Ubatuba) during peace talks.
notes: The poem exists; writing it in the sand is tradition.

C18.title: Portugal becomes Spain (for 60 years)
facts: Iberian Union (1580–1640).
Spain's enemies (Holland, England, France) start attacking Brazil.

C19.title: English pirates in Santos
facts: Thomas Cavendish sacked Santos (1591).
James Lancaster attacked Recife (1595).

C20.title: The Dutch take Salvador
facts: The WIC (Dutch West India Company) took Salvador in 1624.
A Portuguese-Spanish fleet took it back in 1625.

C21.title: Dutch Brazil
facts: The Dutch took Pernambuco (1630), the heart of sugar.
Maurice of Nassau governed from 1637 to 1644: brought painters (Frans Post, Albert Eckhout), scientists, built bridges.
Recife had the first synagogue in the Americas (Kahal Zur Israel).

C22.title: Guararapes
facts: Battles of Guararapes: April 19, 1648 and February 19, 1649.
Leaders: Henrique Dias (Black) and Felipe Camarão/Poti (Potiguar).
April 19 became Brazilian Army Day.

C23.title: Recife's Jews found New York's Jewish community
facts: Dutch surrender in 1654.
The Sephardic Jews of Recife scattered: some went to the Caribbean.
23 reached New Amsterdam in September 1654.

C24.title: Won the war, paid the bill
facts: Peace of The Hague (1661): Portugal paid a huge indemnity (about 4 million cruzados) for Holland to recognize the loss of Brazil.

C25.title: The sugar crisis
facts: In the Antilles, the Dutch, English and French start producing cheaper sugar.
The price collapses. Portugal, already in debt, needs another source of wealth.

C26.title: The privateer who held Rio hostage
facts: Duguay-Trouin took Rio and only left after receiving a ransom in gold, sugar and cattle.

C27.title: Angola Janga
facts: Palmares, in the Serra da Barriga (Alagoas).
Between 6,000 and 20,000 people, several mocambos, capital Macaco.
They farmed and traded. It resisted dozens of expeditions.
notes: Population figures are debated.

C28.title: Ganga Zumba, Zumbi and the betrayal
facts: Ganga Zumba accepted a treaty (1678) and died poisoned; Zumbi took over.
Macaco fell in 1694 to Domingos Jorge Velho's bandeira.
Zumbi was killed on November 20, 1695. Today November 20 is a national holiday (since 2023).
notes: Zumbi's childhood and Ganga Zumba's poisoning are debated.

C29.title: The emerald hunter
facts: Fernão Dias Paes spent 7 years in the backlands, found tourmalines and died in 1681.
He left trails and farm plots that became the infrastructure of the gold rush.
His son-in-law, Borba Gato, killed a Crown official (1682), hid, and later revealed gold on the Rio das Velhas in exchange for a pardon.

C30.title: The gold appears
facts: 1693: Antônio Rodrigues Arzão brings the first official samples.
1698: Antônio Dias de Oliveira finds gold in the Tripuí stream and Ouro Preto is born (the gold was coated in iron oxide and looked black).
Around 1702, João de Siqueira Afonso reaches the area of the future Arraial Velho (Tiradentes).
Around 1704, gold on the Rio das Mortes (São João).

C31.title: Hunger amid the gold
facts: Nobody farmed. Terrible famines in 1697–98 and 1700–01.
The tour text cites a chicken at 140 réis in São Paulo and 4,000 réis in the mines.

C32.title: The rush
facts: Tens of thousands arrive: Paulistas, Bahians, Portuguese and, in greatest numbers, enslaved Africans.
Those from the Mina Coast were valued for their mining experience.
In 1720, Portugal restricted emigration.

C33.title: The Methuen Treaty (“Cloth and Wine”)
facts: Portugal buys English cloth and manufactures; England buys Portuguese wine.
The trade balance is negative for Portugal, which pays the difference in Brazilian gold.
Minas gold helps finance England (and indirectly its Industrial Revolution).
notes: How much the gold weighed in the Industrial Revolution is debated.

C34.title: The Emboaba War
facts: Paulistas × emboabas (Portuguese and “outsiders”).
Emboaba leader: Manuel Nunes Viana, acclaimed “governor” without the king's authorization.
Borba Gato tried to expel him and failed.
notes: The origin of the word “emboaba” is debated.

C35.title: The Capão of Betrayal
facts: Paulistas surrounded in a patch of woods surrendered under a promise of life and were massacred by Bento do Amaral Coutinho's emboabas.
It happened in the Rio das Mortes region (the tour says about 10 km from Tiradentes).
The Paulistas came back with a revenge army (Amador Bueno da Veiga), attacked and withdrew.
notes: The exact place and the death toll are debated.

C36.title: The name “River of the Dead”
facts: The name appears before the war.
Older explanations speak of drownings at crossings and fights with Indigenous peoples.
The war reinforced the legend.
notes: Legend: the link between the name and the Capão. Documented: the name predates the war.

C37.title: The deal that erased the massacre
facts: Creation of the Captaincy of São Paulo and the Gold Mines (1709).
São Paulo becomes a city (1711).
General pardon. Nunes Viana goes back to his farms.

C38.title: The gold towns
facts: Mariana (Ribeirão do Carmo, April 8, the first), Vila Rica (July 8), Sabará (July 17).
The governor named it “Vila Rica de Albuquerque” after himself; the king ordered it changed.

C39.title: Antonil's forbidden book
facts: Cultura e Opulência do Brasil (1711) described the mines and the roads. The Crown seized it.
The line is Antonil's: “Brazil is hell for Blacks, purgatory for whites and paradise for mulattos.”

C40.title: São João del-Rei
facts: Arraial Novo became a town on Dec 8, 1713, honoring King João V.
In 1714, seat of the Rio das Mortes district.
After the gold, it became a trading hub that supplied Rio.
Orchestras from 1776 (Lira Sanjoanense) and the late 18th century (Ribeiro Bastos) still active. “The land where the bells talk.”

C41.title: Town of São José (Tiradentes)
facts: Arraial Velho de Santo Antônio became the Town of São José del-Rei on Jan 19, 1718, by the Count of Assumar, honoring Prince José.
According to the tour, residents pushed for it because more surface gold came out here than in São João.
The Alto São Francisco cross dates from this elevation.

C42.title: Surface gold: easy to find, easy to run out
facts: In Tiradentes the gold was alluvial (streams and banks), not deep-mine gold.
Techniques: the gold pan (bateia) and the mundéu (dams lined with cowhide).
About 80 years of mining at the foot of the ridge (tour data).

C43.title: Smelting houses and the Vila Rica revolt
facts: A 1719 law creates the Smelting Houses: the 20% fifth taken on the spot, gold in stamped bars.
Revolt in June 1720: Pascoal da Silva Guimarães (rich) and Filipe dos Santos (muleteer/commoner).
The Count of Assumar pretends to negotiate, arrests the leaders and burns Pascoal's hill (Morro da Queimada).
Pascoal: arrested and sent to Portugal. Filipe: hanged and quartered in July 1720.
notes: Filipe being dragged by horses is legend.

C44.title: The Captaincy of Minas Gerais is born
facts: Minas is separated from São Paulo; capital: Vila Rica.
First governor: Dom Lourenço de Almeida (1721).
Smelting houses in operation by 1725.

C45.title: The hollow-wood saint
facts: Hollow saint statues filled with gold dust to get past the checkpoints.
notes: The expression exists; large-scale practice is debated.

C46.title: “The fifth from hell”
notes: Linking the expression to the tax is a popular origin story.

C47.title: The Matriz of Santo Antônio
facts: Built from 1710 to 1752; high altar by Portuguese João Ferreira Sampaio.
Portuguese organ with 632 pipes, made in Porto, installed in 1788 according to the tour.
Sundial from 1785; facade design attributed to Aleijadinho (1810).

C48.title: The brotherhoods: one church per group
facts: Matriz / São Francisco / Carmo → “good men” (rich whites, “pure blood”).
Rosário → Africans (with elements of African religions).
Mercês → crioulos (children of Africans born here); São João Evangelista → mulattos/pardos.
Bom Jesus da Pobreza (1782) → whites who became poor.
notes: The general pattern is documented; details of each chapel are debated.

C49.title: Axis of power × axis of servitude
facts: The alleys served for (1) the enslaved to avoid the main streets, (2) access to service areas, (3) draining waste.
70% of the population was enslaved (tour data).
notes: The term “axis of servitude” is the tour's interpretation.

C50.title: Diamonds
facts: Officially announced in 1729.
Tejuco (Diamantina) becomes the Diamond District, under strict control.
Famous figure: Chica da Silva.

C51.title: The capitation: a head tax
facts: A tax per person (including the enslaved), collected twice a year.
So heavy that it was dropped in 1750.

C52.title: The São José fountain
facts: Opened in 1749; shrine with Saint Joseph in boots (patron of the bandeirantes).
Stone aqueduct up to the spring; slightly tilted on purpose, leaning on the aqueduct.
1828 town code with 3 rules: no sharpening machetes, no washing clothes in the front trough, no gatherings with “insolence” toward women.

C53.title: The 100 arrobas
facts: If the fifth didn't reach 100 arrobas (about 1,500 kg), the difference would be collected by force: the derrama.

C54.title: The capital comes down the mountain
facts: Brazil's capital moves from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro in 1763.
Estrada Real: Old Road (Ouro Preto → São João → Paraty) and New Road (Ouro Preto → Rio, shorter, roughly today's BR-040).
Opening another road was a crime of lèse-majesté.

C55.title: The derrama snowball
facts: The tour says there was a derrama in 1763 and that the debt passed 8,600 kg by 1788.
The new governor, Viscount of Barbacena, arrives with orders to collect.

C56.title: The decree that closed the factories
facts: A decree by Queen Maria I banned textile manufacturing in the colony (only coarse cloth for the enslaved escaped).

C57.title: The baptism party (the first meeting)
facts: Father Toledo, the town's vicar, baptized the children of Alvarenga Peixoto and Bárbara Heliodora.
That night there was a party at his house, considered by the tour the first meeting of the conspirators (Oct 10, 1788).
Today the house is the Padre Toledo Museum.
notes: The date and the “first meeting” label are local tradition.

C58.title: The plan
facts: Wait for the derrama, take to the streets, proclaim a republic (Minas and part of Rio).
Capital in São João del-Rei, university in Vila Rica.
Flag with “Libertas quae sera tamen” (today the flag of Minas).
Slavery would not be abolished. Father Toledo owned enslaved people (tour data).

C59.title: The student who went to see Jefferson
facts: José Joaquim da Maia met Jefferson, then US minister to France.
Jefferson was cordial and promised nothing.

C60.title: The plea bargain
facts: Joaquim Silvério dos Reis denounced the group in March 1789.
Barbacena suspended the derrama (no trigger, no revolt) and arrested everyone.
Silvério got his debts forgiven and other benefits.

C61.title: Ten days after Washington
facts: Tiradentes, ensign of the Dragoons regiment, was arrested in Rio on May 10, 1789.

C62.title: Who was Tiradentes
facts: Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, born at Fazenda do Pombal (Ritápolis area, then part of São José).
Orphaned early, self-taught dentist, muleteer, ensign for about 14 years (tour data); patrolled the New Road.
He was the group's propagandist and the only one who admitted his part.

C63.title: The poet dead in his cell
facts: Cláudio Manuel da Costa, at the Casa dos Contos (Ouro Preto).

C64.title: The theater of mercy
facts: Queen Maria I's letter was ready before the sentence.
The others went into exile in Africa (Gonzaga prospered in Mozambique; Alvarenga died in Angola) or to convents (the priests).

C65.title: The gallows
facts: Largo da Lampadosa (today Praça Tiradentes, Rio).
Body parts displayed along the New Road. Declared infamous for generations.
April 21 is a national holiday.

C66.title: The Civic Christ (the invented beard)
facts: Ensigns didn't wear beards (at most a mustache, according to the tour); prisoners had shaved heads.
The Republic (1889) needed a national hero and built a “civic Christ”: a traitor (Judas), apostles, martyrdom.
notes: Documented: the Republic built the image. Legend: the beard.

C67.title: Bom Jesus da Pobreza
facts: Chapel of 1782 on Largo das Forras, a landmark of the decline.
From the late 18th century until the 1970s, the town practically stopped.
notes: The dedication to “poor whites” is the tour's interpretation.

C68.title: The court flees to Brazil
facts: Opening of the ports (1808).
Royal Press: end of the printing ban.
The English reopen mines and bring railways and factories in the 19th century.

C69.title: Does “Uai” come from “why”?
facts: It's folk etymology; linguists link “uai” to Portuguese interjections like “ué”.

C70.title: “For the English to see” and the end of slavery
facts: The 1831 law banning the slave trade was not enforced (the most accepted origin of “para inglês ver”).
The Eusébio de Queirós Law (1850) actually ended the trade.
Free Womb Law (1871); Sexagenarian Law (1885).
Golden Law (May 13, 1888), with no reparations at all.

C71.title: The Confederados
facts: Encouraged by Pedro II, thousands (estimates vary widely; about 10,000 is a common figure) moved to the interior of São Paulo (Americana, Santa Bárbara d'Oeste).
Many came because Brazil still had slavery.
notes: The numbers are debated.

C72.title: The Town of São José becomes Tiradentes
facts: With the Republic, the town is renamed Tiradentes.
Irony: Queen Maria I, who upheld the sentence, was the daughter of José, honored in the old name.

C73.title: Heritage listing
facts: Tiradentes was listed by IPHAN (then SPHAN) in 1938.
Fig trees were planted on Largo das Forras to celebrate (tour data).

C74.title: The Englishman who found Tiradentes
facts: According to the tour: John Parsons opened the Solar da Ponte (1972).
In the 80s he helped families restore old mansions and fought for underground wiring; he died in 2016.
notes: Local data (tour text).

C75.title: Burle Marx, Globo and the boom
facts: According to the tour: Burle Marx gardens on Largo das Forras (1980s).
Yves Alves (Globo director) and the Roberto Marinho Foundation restored Rua Direita; the town became a soap-opera set in the 90s.
Today: almost 200 inns and the Film Festival (since 1998).
notes: Local data (tour text).

EXP-lavar-egua.legend: The enslaved hid gold in the mud on the mares' backs and then washed the animals.

EXP-burros-agua.legend: Bandeirantes and muleteers lost mules at river crossings.

EXP-picar-mula.legend: Spurring the stubborn mule to get it moving.

EXP-ingles-ver.legend: Decoy ships to fool the English.

buck.role: Protagonist · “The Highlander of the Royal Road”
buck.visual: Brown Stetson with the front brim bent up; red plaid shirt with rolled sleeves; leather vest; blue bandana; boots with star spurs; a dented tin canteen on the left side of his belt.
buck.function: A Nashville cowboy (1876) stuck in time after drinking from the fountain. Compares everything to the US and is confidently wrong.

mula.visual: A gray-brown mule with a leather pack saddle and two chests; a blue flame where the head should be; a gold earring floating where the ear would be.
mula.function: The Brazilian voice and the hint button. Stops joking on serious cards.
mula.catchphrase: Here even the tax has 300 years of tradition.

cobrador.visual: Tall, dark-blue frock coat with gold buttons, white wig with a queue, tricorn; ledger chained to his wrist and a gold scale; eyes like crown seals.
cobrador.function: Takes 20% of all the player's gold and triggers the Derrama. He isn't a person: he's a system.

sineiro.visual: An elderly Black man, white cotton shirt, rolled-up trousers, barefoot, holding a thick bell rope that comes down from the sky.
sineiro.function: Gives the missions by ringing bells (mission, correct, danger, achievement). Lives in São João del-Rei.
sineiro.catchphrase: Here the bell talks. You just have to learn to listen.

quitandeira.name: The freed food seller
quitandeira.function: Sells food at the camp entrance and trades clues for coins. Symbol of purchased freedom.

tropeiro.name: The muleteer
tropeiro.function: The Brazilian cowboy; the protagonist's mirror.

antonil.function: Wrote too much and had his book seized.

tiradentes.role: NPC · Joaquim José da Silva Xavier
tiradentes.function: The Conspiracy's propagandist; the beard was invented later.

Q01.prompt: How many ships did Columbus take in 1492?
Q01.explain: Santa María, Pinta and Niña, with about 90 men.

Q02.prompt: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) split the world between…
Q02.explain: A line 370 leagues west of Cape Verde: west for Spain, east for Portugal.

Q03.prompt: Who touched the Northeast coast before Cabral, in January 1500?
Q03.explain: Former captain of the Niña. By the treaty, the land belonged to Portugal.

Q04.prompt: Where did Cabral's fleet land on April 22, 1500?
Q04.explain: 13 ships, about 1,500 men. He thought it was an island.

Q05.prompt: Why is Rio de Janeiro called that?
options: They found the bay in January and thought it was a river
In honor of a saint named January
It was the name of a ship
Q05.explain: The 1501–1502 expedition, with Vespucci, named places by the calendar.

Q06.prompt: Where does the name “pau-brasil” come from?
options: From a Tupi word for tree
Q06.explain: The red dye was valuable for cloth in Europe.

Q10.prompt: What was Brazil's first official town (1532)?
Q10.explain: Founded by Martim Afonso de Sousa, 75 years before Jamestown.

Q12.prompt: What was Brazil's first capital, founded in 1549?
Q12.explain: Tomé de Sousa. It was the capital for 214 years.

Q13.prompt: What share of the whole Atlantic slave trade came to Brazil?

Q16.prompt: Rio de Janeiro was founded in 1565 to drive out whom?
Q16.explain: Villegaignon's France Antarctique, in Guanabara Bay.

Q21.prompt: Who governed Dutch Recife from 1637 to 1644?
Q21.explain: He brought painters and scientists and built bridges.

Q23.prompt: How many Jewish refugees from Recife reached New Amsterdam in 1654?
Q23.explain: The first Jewish community in New York.

Q29.prompt: Fernão Dias died believing he had emeralds. They were…
Q29.explain: But his trails became the infrastructure of the gold rush.

options: The gold was coated in iron oxide and looked black
The gold was burned at the foundry
Q30.explain: Antônio Dias de Oliveira, Tripuí stream, 1698.

Q33.prompt: In the Methuen Treaty (1703), England bought wine. Portugal bought…
Q33.explain: The difference was paid in Brazilian gold.

Q34.prompt: In the Emboaba War, the Paulistas fought against…

Q41.prompt: When did the camp become the Town of São José (today Tiradentes)?
Q41.explain: By the Count of Assumar, honoring Prince José.

Q43a.prompt: After the Vila Rica revolt (1720), who was hanged?
Q43a.explain: The rich man (Pascoal) was sent to Portugal. The poor man got the rope.

Q43b.prompt: How many years before the Boston Tea Party (1773) was the gold revolt (1720)?
Q43b.explain: Yours was about tea. Ours was about gold.

Q47.prompt: How long did it take to build the Matriz de Santo Antônio?

Q48a.prompt: Whose brotherhood was the Rosário church?

Q48b.prompt: Whose brotherhood was the São João Evangelista church?
Q48b.explain: Mercês = crioulos; Rosário = Africans; Matriz/Carmo = rich whites.

Q52.prompt: When was the São José fountain opened?
Q52.explain: Drinking water, horse trough and laundry.

Q53.prompt: What yearly quota for the fifth was set in 1750?
Q53.explain: If it wasn't met, the derrama came.

Q54.prompt: In what year did Brazil's capital move to Rio de Janeiro?
Q54.explain: The gold went down the mountain; the capital followed it.

Q58a.prompt: What would be the capital of the conspirators' republic?
Q58a.explain: And the university would be in Vila Rica.

Q58b.prompt: Did the conspirators' plan abolish slavery?
Q58b.explain: Like the Founding Fathers: they talked about liberty and owned slaves.

Q59.prompt: Who did José Joaquim da Maia meet in France in 1787?
Q59.explain: Jefferson was cordial and promised nothing.

Q60.explain: He traded his friends for having his debts forgiven.

Q61a.prompt: How many days after George Washington's inauguration was Tiradentes arrested?
Q61a.explain: Washington took office on April 30, 1789; Tiradentes was arrested on May 10, 1789.

Q65.explain: Largo da Lampadosa, Rio. Today it's a national holiday.

Q66.prompt: Who created the image of the bearded, Christ-like Tiradentes?
Q66.explain: Ensigns didn't wear beards, and prisoners had shaved heads.

Q70a.prompt: What was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery?
Q70a.explain: Golden Law, May 13, 1888, with no reparations.

Q70b.prompt: What is the most accepted origin of “para inglês ver” (for the English to see)?
options: The 1831 anti-trade law that was never enforced
Q70b.explain: 1831 = “for the English to see”. 1850 = the law that stuck.

Q72.prompt: In what year was the Town of São José renamed Tiradentes?
Q72.explain: With the Republic. Queen Maria I was the daughter of José.

Q73.prompt: In what year was Tiradentes listed by IPHAN (then SPHAN)?
Q73.explain: Poverty saved the town: nobody had money to tear anything down.

Q74.prompt: Who opened the Solar da Ponte in 1972, according to the tour?
Q74.explain: An English engineer. Everyone thought he was crazy.

F01.prompt: The Rio das Mortes got its name from the bodies of the Capão da Traição.
F01.explain: The name appears before the war. The war only reinforced the legend.

F02.explain: Folk etymology. Linguists link “uai” to interjections like “ué”.

F03.prompt: Hollow wooden saints full of gold were used on a large scale to fool the tax man.
F03.explain: The expression exists; large-scale practice is debated.

F04.prompt: Anchieta wrote a 5,000-line poem in the sand on the beach.
F04.explain: The poem exists; writing it in the sand is tradition.

F05.prompt: Tiradentes had a long beard when he was arrested.
F05.explain: The beard was created by the Republic, a hundred years later.

F06.prompt: Filipe dos Santos was dragged by horses.
F06.explain: Documented: hanged and quartered. Being dragged by horses is legend.

F07.prompt: The expression “quinto dos infernos” (fifth from hell) was born from the fifth tax.

F08.prompt: The most accepted explanation for “para inglês ver” is an 1831 law that was never enforced.
F08.explain: The law banned the slave trade and stayed on paper.

F09.prompt: New York's first Jewish community came from Recife.
F09.explain: 23 refugees reached New Amsterdam in September 1654.

F10.prompt: A Brazilian student asked Thomas Jefferson for help in 1787.
F10.explain: José Joaquim da Maia. Jefferson promised nothing.

F11.prompt: Tiradentes was arrested ten days after George Washington's inauguration.

F12.prompt: The first Europeans to stay in Brazil were two convicts and two runaway cabin boys.
F12.explain: Cabral left the convicts; the cabin boys ran away.

F13.prompt: Ouro Preto's gold looked black because it was coated in iron oxide.

F14.prompt: “Lavar a égua” (to wash the mare) comes from enslaved people hiding gold in the mud on mares' backs.

F15.prompt: “Pé-rapado” (scraped foot) comes from the boot scrapers at church doors.

F16.prompt: Dutch Recife had the first synagogue in the Americas.

F17.prompt: The conspirators planned to abolish slavery.
F17.explain: False: slavery would not be abolished.

F18.prompt: Minas gold helped pay for Portugal's purchases in England.
F18.explain: Methuen Treaty (1703): the trade gap was paid in gold.

F19.prompt: The Matriz de Santo Antônio took 42 years to finish.

F20.prompt: “Subir na vida” (to climb in life) comes from townhouses built floor by floor.

F21.prompt: The São José fountain is slightly tilted on purpose.
F21.explain: It leans on the aqueduct. “A listed building, literally leaning.”

paths.cap1.title: Chapter 1 · Brazilwood
paths.cap1.scenes.0.title: Tiradentes · today
paths.cap1.scenes.0.lines.2.text: I wouldn't drink that, cowboy. This fountain is drinking water, horse trough and laundry.
paths.cap1.scenes.0.lines.4.text: The sky spins. The canteen turns ice-cold. Buck Calhoun is stuck in time.
paths.cap1.scenes.1.title: The Lookout
paths.cap1.scenes.1.lines.0.text: Here the bell talks. You just have to learn to listen.
paths.cap1.scenes.1.lines.1.text: This is the Lookout. Cross from 1718, when the camp became a town. There, the Serra de São José: the gold came from it.
paths.cap1.scenes.1.lines.3.text: Modern history starts in 1500. Here, nothing for 200 years. Then everything at once.
paths.cap1.scenes.1.lines.4.text: To understand this town, you'll have to go back to the beginning.
paths.cap1.scenes.1.lines.5.text: Grab your canteen. We're going by caravel.
paths.cap1.scenes.2.title: Era 0 · The World Before Brazil
paths.cap1.scenes.2.lines.0.text: 1492. A Genoese sailor with 3 ships reaches the Bahamas thinking he's in Asia.
paths.cap1.scenes.2.lines.2.text: And it was on that voyage that Europeans learned the Taíno word barbacoa.
paths.cap1.scenes.2.lines.4.text: 1494, Tordesillas: Spain and Portugal split the planet. West for Spain, east for Portugal.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.title: Lisbon · March 1500
paths.cap1.scenes.3.intro: Cabral leaves Lisbon for India with 13 ships and about 1,500 men. You're at the helm.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.0.options.0.label: South, down along Africa
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.0.options.0.reply: Right. First the Canaries, then Cape Verde.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.0.options.1.label: West, straight into open sea
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.0.options.1.reply: Too soon, cowboy. First go down the African coast.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.1.prompt: After Cape Verde, the road to India goes around Africa. How do you make the turn?
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.1.options.0.label: Hugging the African coast
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.1.options.0.reply: Then you get stuck. Make that turn wider.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.1.options.1.label: Swing a wide turn to the west
paths.cap1.scenes.3.legs.1.options.1.reply: Wide turn… too wide. There's something up ahead.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.egg.lines.0.text: Psst. In January 1500 a Spaniard had already been here: Pinzón, former captain of Columbus's Niña.
paths.cap1.scenes.3.egg.lines.2.text: By the treaty, it belonged to Portugal. He found it, but didn't get to keep it.
paths.cap1.scenes.4.title: April 22, 1500 · Porto Seguro
paths.cap1.scenes.4.lines.1.text: And he thought it was an island. Named it the Island of Vera Cruz.
paths.cap1.scenes.5.text: Cabral needs to tell the king. Now what?
paths.cap1.scenes.5.options.0.label: Send a ship back with Pero Vaz de Caminha's letter
paths.cap1.scenes.5.options.0.reply.0.text: That's exactly it. One ship went back with the letter, and the rest of the fleet sailed on to India.
paths.cap1.scenes.5.options.1.label: Stay and found a town
paths.cap1.scenes.5.options.1.reply.0.text: Easy. The first town only comes 32 years later. The letter goes back on one ship; the fleet sails on to India.
paths.cap1.scenes.6.lines.0.text: They left behind 2 convicts. And 2 cabin boys ran away and stayed too.
paths.cap1.scenes.7.title: AGE I · The Brazilwood Age
paths.cap1.scenes.7.lines.0.text: 1501. An expedition with Amerigo Vespucci sails up the coast naming everything after the saint of the day.
paths.cap1.scenes.7.lines.2.text: That's the one. Now it's your turn: name the places by the calendar.
paths.cap1.scenes.8.rounds.0.place: A huge bay on the coast of Bahia.
paths.cap1.scenes.8.rounds.1.place: A bay so enclosed it looks like a river mouth.
paths.cap1.scenes.9.lines.0.text: The land's first business: brazilwood, a red dye prized in Europe. The name comes from “brasa”, ember.
paths.cap1.scenes.9.lines.2.text: The Crown leases the trade to Fernão de Noronha. Indigenous people cut and carry, for tools and cloth: barter.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.intro: The ship needs 12 brazilwood logs. You negotiate. The village's trust matters.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.0.label: Iron axes
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.0.line: Good tools. A fair trade, and the village trusts you more.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.1.label: Cloth
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.2.label: Little mirrors
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.2.line: Gets you logs today, but the village realizes it got the short end.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.3.label: Promises in the Crown's name
paths.cap1.scenes.10.offers.3.line: The Crown promises a lot and delivers little. The village isn't fooled.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.win.0.text: 12 logs, and the village still trusts you. Fair trade builds alliances.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.lose.0.text: The trust is gone. Abusive trade turned into conflict.
paths.cap1.scenes.10.after.0.text: In real life, barter became exploitation. Sugar brought Indigenous enslavement. Then African.
paths.cap1.scenes.11.intro: To store the logs until the next ship, Portugal builds a fortified trading post: the feitoria.
paths.cap1.scenes.11.button: Build the Cabo Frio trading post
paths.cap1.scenes.11.lines.0.text: The oldest on record stood near Cabo Frio, with about 24 men.
paths.cap1.scenes.12.lines.0.text: A Portuguese man was shipwrecked here and stayed. The Indigenous people call him Caramuru.
paths.cap1.scenes.12.lines.1.text: I was shipwrecked, I stayed and I married Paraguaçu. Want to trade with the village? First learn how to arrive.
paths.cap1.scenes.13.text: How do you arrive at a village?
paths.cap1.scenes.13.options.0.label: With a gift, listening before talking
paths.cap1.scenes.13.options.0.reply.0.text: That's how you build an alliance.
paths.cap1.scenes.13.options.1.label: Giving orders in the king's name
paths.cap1.scenes.13.options.1.reply.0.text: The king is an ocean away, cowboy. Try again, politely.
paths.cap1.scenes.14.lines.0.text: Paraguaçu is baptized in France in 1528: Catarina. Farther south, João Ramalho marries Bartira, daughter of chief Tibiriçá.
paths.cap1.scenes.14.lines.3.text: Except here it really happened, with dozens of children.
paths.cap1.scenes.14.lines.4.text: 1524: castaway Aleixo Garcia walks from the Atlantic to the Incas on the Peabiru, 3,000 km of Guarani trail. Dies on the way back.
paths.cap1.scenes.15.title: The bell rings
paths.cap1.scenes.15.intro: To move on to the next era, show what you learned. Get 2 out of 3.
paths.cap1.scenes.16.text: Next era: Age II · Sugar & Blood.
paths.cap2.title: Chapter 2 · Sugar & Blood
paths.cap2.scenes.0.title: AGE II · Sugar & Blood
paths.cap2.scenes.0.lines.0.text: 1532. After 32 years of “we'll see later”, Portugal founds its first town: São Vicente.
paths.cap2.scenes.0.lines.2.text: The founder was Martim Afonso de Sousa. One of the first sugar mills stood nearby.
paths.cap2.scenes.1.rounds.0.place: An official town needs a local government. Which one?
paths.cap2.scenes.1.rounds.1.place: And the symbol of the king's justice, the stone column in the square. Which one?
paths.cap2.scenes.1.rounds.1.after: Council and pillory: São Vicente was Brazil's first official town.
paths.cap2.scenes.2.text: 1534. Giant colony, empty treasury. The coast becomes strips for grantees. Pick yours:
paths.cap2.scenes.2.options.0.label: Pernambuco, Duarte Coelho's
paths.cap2.scenes.2.options.0.reply.0.text: It worked, thanks to sugar. One of the very few.
paths.cap2.scenes.2.options.1.label: Any strip of coast
paths.cap2.scenes.2.options.1.reply.0.text: Bankrupt. Almost all of them went bankrupt.
paths.cap2.scenes.2.options.2.label: São Vicente
paths.cap2.scenes.3.lines.1.text: Tomé de Sousa founds Salvador, the first capital. With him, the first Jesuits.
paths.cap2.scenes.4.title: The sugar mill
paths.cap2.scenes.4.lines.0.text: This is where I stop joking.
paths.cap2.scenes.4.lines.1.text: Sugar needed hands. First they enslaved the Indigenous peoples, the so-called “negros da terra”.
paths.cap2.scenes.4.lines.2.text: Epidemics, Indigenous resistance, Jesuit pressure and the profits of the trade: African slavery grows.
paths.cap2.scenes.4.lines.3.text: Brazil received about 4.8 million enslaved Africans: close to 40% of the Atlantic trade.
paths.cap2.scenes.5.lines.0.text: German Hans Staden is captured by the Tupinambá. Months awaiting ritual execution. And he escapes.
paths.cap2.scenes.6.lines.1.text: Bishop Sardinha. Shipwrecked in Alagoas, killed by the Caeté. His name meant Sardine: I'm just reporting.
paths.cap2.scenes.6.lines.2.text: The Crown's response was no joke at all: it authorized the enslavement of the Caeté.
paths.cap2.scenes.7.lines.0.text: Villegaignon's Frenchmen found France Antarctique in Guanabara Bay.
paths.cap2.scenes.7.lines.1.text: The Tupinambá of the Tamoio Confederation, with Cunhambebe and Aimberê, ally with the French.
paths.cap2.scenes.8.text: How does Portugal get the French out of Guanabara?
paths.cap2.scenes.8.options.0.label: By founding a city right there
paths.cap2.scenes.8.options.0.reply.0.text: Right. Estácio de Sá founds Rio on March 1, 1565. The French leave for good in 1567.
paths.cap2.scenes.8.options.0.reply.2.text: And the Temiminó Arariboia, a Portuguese ally, founds Niterói.
paths.cap2.scenes.8.options.1.label: By asking politely
paths.cap2.scenes.8.options.1.reply.0.text: With the French? In 1555? Try again.
paths.cap2.scenes.9.lines.0.text: The Jesuit Anchieta is held hostage by the Tamoio at Iperoig, today Ubatuba, negotiating peace.
paths.cap2.scenes.9.lines.2.text: Tale! The poem exists; writing it in the sand is tradition. On the tour: “they say…”.
paths.cap2.scenes.10.title: The bell rings
paths.cap2.scenes.10.intro: To move on to the next era, get 2 out of 3.
paths.cap2.scenes.11.text: Next era: Age III · Everybody Wants a Piece.
paths.cap3.title: Chapter 3 · Everybody Wants a Piece
paths.cap3.scenes.0.title: AGE III · Everybody Wants a Piece
paths.cap3.scenes.0.lines.0.text: 1580. Portugal's king dies in Morocco without an heir. Spain inherits Portugal…
paths.cap3.scenes.0.lines.2.text: The Iberian Union, from 1580 to 1640. Holland, England and France start attacking Brazil.
paths.cap3.scenes.1.lines.0.text: English pirate Thomas Cavendish sacks Santos. In 1595, James Lancaster attacks Recife.
paths.cap3.scenes.2.lines.0.text: The Dutch West India Company, the WIC, takes Salvador, the capital.
paths.cap3.scenes.2.lines.1.text: In 1625, a huge Portuguese and Spanish fleet takes the city back.
paths.cap3.scenes.3.title: 1630–1654 · Dutch Recife
paths.cap3.scenes.3.lines.0.text: 1630: the Dutch come back and take Pernambuco, the heart of sugar.
paths.cap3.scenes.3.lines.1.text: Nassau (1637–1644): painters like Frans Post, scientists, bridges. And the first synagogue in the Americas.
paths.cap3.scenes.3.lines.3.text: At the same time, the Dutch held New Amsterdam, the future New York. Remember that.
paths.cap3.scenes.4.text: Who defeats the Dutch at Guararapes?
paths.cap3.scenes.4.options.0.label: Portuguese, Indigenous and Black soldiers, side by side
paths.cap3.scenes.4.options.0.reply.0.text: Right. Leaders: Henrique Dias, Black, and Felipe Camarão, Potiguar. Battles in 1648 and 1649.
paths.cap3.scenes.4.options.1.label: Only the Spanish fleet
paths.cap3.scenes.4.options.1.reply.0.text: That was 1625, in Salvador. This time it was other people. Try again.
paths.cap3.scenes.5.egg.label: 🌀 Secret Time Gate
paths.cap3.scenes.5.egg.lines.0.text: September 1654 · New Amsterdam. Windmills, a wooden fort, Dutch houses.
paths.cap3.scenes.5.egg.lines.1.text: 23 Jewish refugees from Recife land here. They become the first Jewish community in New York.
paths.cap3.scenes.5.egg.lines.3.text: On a corner, a sign: Wall Street (under construction).
paths.cap3.scenes.5.lines.0.text: 1654: the Dutch surrender. The Sephardic Jews of Recife scatter; some go to the Caribbean.
paths.cap3.scenes.5.lines.1.text: And 23 of them reach New Amsterdam in September 1654.
paths.cap3.scenes.6.title: 1661 · Peace of The Hague
paths.cap3.scenes.6.lines.1.text: About 4 million cruzados in indemnity for Holland to recognize the loss of Brazil.
paths.cap3.scenes.7.lines.0.text: The Dutch, English and French make cheaper sugar in the Caribbean. The price collapses.
paths.cap3.scenes.7.lines.2.text: Portugal, deep in debt, needs another source of wealth. The arrow on the map points inland…
paths.cap3.scenes.8.lines.0.text: French privateer Duguay-Trouin takes Rio and only leaves with a ransom of gold, sugar and cattle.
paths.cap3.scenes.9.lines.1.text: For almost 100 years, a free Black state in the Serra da Barriga, Alagoas: Palmares, Angola Janga.
paths.cap3.scenes.9.lines.2.text: 6,000 to 20,000 people, several mocambos. They farmed, traded and resisted dozens of expeditions.
paths.cap3.scenes.10.lines.0.text: 1678: Ganga Zumba accepts a treaty and dies poisoned. Zumbi takes over.
paths.cap3.scenes.10.lines.1.text: 1694: Macaco falls to Domingos Jorge Velho's bandeira.
paths.cap3.scenes.10.lines.2.text: November 20, 1695: Zumbi is killed. Today, November 20 is a national holiday.
paths.cap3.scenes.10.lines.3.text: One toll of the bell. In silence.
paths.cap3.scenes.11.title: The bell rings
paths.cap3.scenes.11.intro: To move on to the next era, get 2 out of 3.
paths.cap3.scenes.12.text: Next era: Age IV · The Gold Age.
paths.cap4.title: Chapter 4 · The Gold Age
paths.cap4.scenes.0.title: AGE IV · The Gold Age
paths.cap4.scenes.0.lines.0.text: 1674. Fernão Dias spends 7 years hunting emeralds. Dies happy with some green stones.
paths.cap4.scenes.0.lines.2.text: His son-in-law, Borba Gato, killed a Crown official and hid. He traded gold on the Rio das Velhas for a pardon.
paths.cap4.scenes.1.title: 1693–1698 · Gold appears
paths.cap4.scenes.1.intro: Tap the gold pan to swirl and wash the stream gravel.
paths.cap4.scenes.1.lines.0.text: 1693: Arzão brings the first samples. 1698: gold in the Tripuí, coated in iron oxide. It looks black: Ouro Preto.
paths.cap4.scenes.1.lines.2.text: Notice the stamp: 20% already went to the Collector.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.title: 1697 · The rush
paths.cap4.scenes.2.intro: Take your pack train to the mines. Every leg uses up food.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.0.text: Bring food for the trip, or only mining tools?
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.0.options.0.label: Food
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.0.options.0.reply: Good call. In the mines, nobody farms.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.0.options.1.label: Only tools
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.1.text: The trail is packed: Paulistas, Bahians, Portuguese and, in greatest numbers, enslaved Africans.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.1.options.0.label: Keep going
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.1.options.0.reply: Tens of thousands take the same road.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.2.text: Terrible famine: nobody planted. Food is worth gold.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.2.options.0.label: Trade gold for food
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.2.options.0.reply: People starved to death with gold in their pockets.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.legs.2.options.1.label: Pan for more gold
paths.cap4.scenes.2.end.0.text: The famines of 1697–98 and 1700–01 were real.
paths.cap4.scenes.2.end.2.text: So many people came that, in 1720, Portugal restricted emigration.
paths.cap4.scenes.3.egg.lines.0.text: An invisible pipe runs out of your treasury, dripping gold all the way to a ship flying the English flag.
paths.cap4.scenes.3.lines.0.text: The Methuen Treaty: England buys Portuguese wine; Portugal buys English cloth.
paths.cap4.scenes.3.lines.1.text: The difference? Paid in Brazilian gold. It helped finance England.
paths.cap4.scenes.4.title: 1707 · Emboabas
paths.cap4.scenes.4.text: Brazil's first civil war: Paulistas, who found the gold, against emboabas, who came later. Your side?
paths.cap4.scenes.4.options.0.label: Paulistas
paths.cap4.scenes.4.options.0.reply.0.text: The Paulistas mocked the outsiders in boots. Emboaba may be a bird with feathered legs.
paths.cap4.scenes.4.options.1.label: Emboabas
paths.cap4.scenes.4.options.1.reply.0.text: Emboaba Nunes Viana made himself “governor” without the king's say. Borba Gato tried to expel him and failed.
paths.cap4.scenes.5.title: 1709 · The Capão of Betrayal
paths.cap4.scenes.5.lines.0.text: Paulistas surrounded in a patch of woods surrender under a promise of life.
paths.cap4.scenes.5.lines.1.text: Massacred by the emboabas at the Rio das Mortes. The tour says: about 10 km from Tiradentes.
paths.cap4.scenes.6.title: River of the Dead
paths.cap4.scenes.6.lines.1.text: Tale! The name predates the war: drownings, fights with Indigenous peoples. The war only fed the legend.
paths.cap4.scenes.7.lines.0.text: Nobody was punished. A general pardon and a new captaincy: São Paulo and the Gold Mines.
paths.cap4.scenes.7.lines.2.text: 1711: Mariana, Vila Rica and Sabará are born. The governor put his own name on one… and the king had it removed.
paths.cap4.scenes.8.title: 1711 · The forbidden book
paths.cap4.scenes.8.lines.0.text: I wrote Cultura e Opulência do Brasil: the mines, the roads, all the wealth.
paths.cap4.scenes.8.lines.1.text: And the Crown seized the book. He said too much. In Brazil even printing presses were banned: only allowed from 1808.
paths.cap4.scenes.8.lines.2.text: “Brazil is hell for Blacks, purgatory for whites and paradise for mulattos.”
paths.cap4.scenes.8.lines.3.text: The line is his, from 1711. On the tour, at São João Evangelista, we discuss why it's complicated.
paths.cap4.scenes.9.lines.0.text: 1713: Arraial Novo becomes São João del-Rei, honoring King João V. Here the bells talk.
paths.cap4.scenes.9.lines.1.text: When the gold ran out, the town survived by selling, praying and playing music.
paths.cap4.scenes.9.lines.2.text: January 19, 1718: Arraial Velho becomes the Town of São José del-Rei, for Prince José.
paths.cap4.scenes.9.lines.4.text: Today that town is called Tiradentes.
paths.cap4.scenes.10.title: Surface gold
paths.cap4.scenes.10.intro: Here the gold was alluvial: streams and banks. Swirl the gold pan!
paths.cap4.scenes.10.lines.0.text: Gold pan and mundéu, dams lined with cowhide. About 80 years of mining at the foot of the ridge.
paths.cap4.scenes.10.lines.2.text: Easy to find, easy to run out.
paths.cap4.scenes.11.lines.0.text: No more gold dust. All of it goes to the Smelting House: melted, stamped, the fifth taken on the spot.
paths.cap4.scenes.11.lines.1.text: June 1720: revolt in Vila Rica, led by rich Pascoal da Silva and muleteer Filipe dos Santos.
paths.cap4.scenes.11.lines.2.text: The Count of Assumar fakes talks, arrests the leaders and burns Pascoal's hill: the Morro da Queimada.
paths.cap4.scenes.11.lines.4.text: Remember this pattern: it returns in 1792. Your Tea Party was about tea; ours, gold, 53 years earlier. Yours worked.
paths.cap4.scenes.12.title: December 2, 1720
paths.cap4.scenes.12.lines.0.text: The Captaincy of Minas Gerais is born. Capital: Vila Rica.
paths.cap4.scenes.12.lines.2.text: People called the tax “the fifth from hell”… so they say. And hid gold in hollow saints… so they say.
paths.cap4.scenes.13.title: The bell rings
paths.cap4.scenes.13.intro: To move on to the next era, get 2 out of 3.
paths.cap4.scenes.14.text: Next era: Age V · Peak & Segregation.
paths.cap5.title: Chapter 5 · Peak & Segregation
paths.cap5.scenes.0.title: AGE V · Peak & Segregation
paths.cap5.scenes.0.lines.0.text: 1710 to 1752: the Matriz de Santo Antônio. 42 years of construction.
paths.cap5.scenes.0.lines.2.text: According to local records. Ouro Preto says theirs is second… but counts the silver. We don't.
paths.cap5.scenes.1.title: One church per group
paths.cap5.scenes.1.rounds.2.options.0: Crioulos: children of Africans born here
paths.cap5.scenes.2.title: Two towns in one
paths.cap5.scenes.2.intro: Illustrative map. Switch between street and alley and visit the spots.
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.0.label: The Matriz, at the top
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.0.lines.0.text: The church of the “good men”, at the highest point of the town.
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.1.label: The main street
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.1.lines.0.text: Sobrado: shop downstairs, family upstairs. The street was the axis of power.
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.2.label: The fountain
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.2.lines.0.text: The 1749 fountain: water, horse trough and laundry.
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.3.label: Alley beside the Matriz
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.3.lines.0.text: The alleys: a path for the enslaved away from main streets, access to back yards, and waste drainage.
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.4.label: Little stairway between houses
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.4.lines.0.text: According to the tour, 70% of the population was enslaved.
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.5.label: Back alley
paths.cap5.scenes.2.spots.5.lines.1.text: Even today you can cross the whole town without touching a main street.
paths.cap5.scenes.3.lines.0.text: Diamonds! Tejuco, today Diamantina, becomes the Diamond District, locked down by the Crown.
paths.cap5.scenes.3.lines.2.text: The famous figure there is Chica da Silva. That's for another phase.
paths.cap5.scenes.4.lines.0.text: A new tax: per head. Every person pays, including every enslaved person. Twice a year.
paths.cap5.scenes.4.lines.2.text: It was so heavy it was dropped in 1750.
paths.cap5.scenes.5.title: 1749 · The fountain
paths.cap5.scenes.5.lines.0.text: The biggest colonial fountain in Minas, with Saint Joseph in boots in the shrine, patron of the bandeirantes.
paths.cap5.scenes.5.lines.1.text: Slightly tilted on purpose, leaning on the stone aqueduct that runs up to the spring.
paths.cap5.scenes.6.title: 1750 · The 100 arrobas
paths.cap5.scenes.6.lines.0.text: The quota: 100 arrobas of gold a year. About 1,500 kilos.
paths.cap5.scenes.6.lines.1.text: Came up short? The difference will be collected by force. It's called the derrama.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.title: 1763 · The Estrada Real
paths.cap5.scenes.7.intro: The gold goes down the mountain to Rio, and the capital follows it. Take the pack train from Vila Rica to Rio.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.0.text: Two official roads: the Old one, via São João to Paraty, and the New one, shorter, to Rio.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.0.options.0.label: New Road
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.0.options.0.reply: Shorter. Today it's roughly the BR-040 highway.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.0.options.1.label: Cut a shortcut through the forest
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.0.options.1.reply: Opening another road was a crime of lèse-majesté! You lost a mule coming back.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.1.text: A tax post. The inspector looks at the cargo.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.1.options.0.label: Pay the Fifth
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.1.options.1.label: Hide gold in a wooden saint
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.1.options.1.reply: The inspector knocked on the saint: hollow. You paid the Fifth anyway.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.2.options.0.label: Wait for the rain to pass
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.2.options.1.label: Cross the river with the mules
paths.cap5.scenes.7.legs.2.options.1.reply: The mules went into the water. They say the expression “dar com os burros n'água” comes from this… it's a tale.
paths.cap5.scenes.7.end.0.text: The muleteers were Brazil's mule cowboys.
paths.cap5.scenes.8.title: The bell rings
paths.cap5.scenes.8.intro: To move on to the next era, get 2 out of 3.
paths.cap5.scenes.9.text: Next era: Age VI · The Conspiracy.
paths.cap6.title: Chapter 6 · The Conspiracy
paths.cap6.scenes.0.title: AGE VI · The Conspiracy
paths.cap6.scenes.0.lines.0.text: Every year the quota was missed. Every year the debt rolled over to the next.
paths.cap6.scenes.0.lines.2.text: Then the new governor arrives, the Viscount of Barbacena, with orders to collect.
paths.cap6.scenes.1.lines.0.text: Queen Maria I bans textile making in Brazil. Only coarse cloth for the enslaved is left.
paths.cap6.scenes.2.title: October 10, 1788
paths.cap6.scenes.2.text: Father Toledo baptized the children of Alvarenga Peixoto and Bárbara Heliodora. Party that night. Which group do you join?
paths.cap6.scenes.2.options.0.label: The group by the window
paths.cap6.scenes.2.options.0.reply.0.text: “…wait for the derrama… when the people are angry, we take to the streets…”
paths.cap6.scenes.2.options.1.label: The group by the harpsichord
paths.cap6.scenes.2.options.1.reply.0.text: “…a republic… a university in Vila Rica… and the capital in São João del-Rei…”
paths.cap6.scenes.2.options.2.label: I've heard enough
paths.cap6.scenes.2.options.2.reply.0.text: Tradition says: the conspirators' first meeting. Today the house is the Padre Toledo Museum.
paths.cap6.scenes.3.title: The plan
paths.cap6.scenes.3.text: A republic in Minas, a university, a flag reading “Libertas quae sera tamen”. Vote:
paths.cap6.scenes.3.options.0.label: Abolish slavery
paths.cap6.scenes.3.options.0.reply.0.text: Locked option. The conspirators weren't going to abolish slavery. Father Toledo owned enslaved people, says the tour.
paths.cap6.scenes.3.options.1.label: Approve the plan as it was
paths.cap6.scenes.3.options.1.reply.0.text: “Libertas quae sera tamen”: today it's the flag of Minas.
paths.cap6.scenes.4.lines.0.text: Two years earlier, student José Joaquim da Maia goes to see Thomas Jefferson in France.
paths.cap6.scenes.4.lines.2.text: He was cordial. And promised nothing.
paths.cap6.scenes.5.title: March 1789
paths.cap6.scenes.5.lines.0.text: I owed the Crown a fortune. I traded my friends for my debt.
paths.cap6.scenes.5.lines.1.text: Silvério dos Reis denounces the group. Barbacena calls off the derrama: no trigger, no revolt. And arrests them all.
paths.cap6.scenes.5.lines.2.text: You lost the mission. On purpose: so did they. And Silvério got his debts forgiven.
paths.cap6.scenes.6.title: May 10, 1789
paths.cap6.scenes.6.lines.2.text: Joaquim José da Silva Xavier. Self-taught dentist, muleteer, ensign. I patrolled the New Road.
paths.cap6.scenes.6.lines.3.text: He was the group's propagandist. And the only one who admitted everything.
paths.cap6.scenes.7.lines.0.text: The poet Cláudio Manuel da Costa is found dead in his cell. Suicide or murder? Still debated.
paths.cap6.scenes.7.lines.1.text: 1792: eleven sentenced to death. Then the queen's mercy arrives… written before the sentence.
paths.cap6.scenes.7.lines.3.text: Gonzaga prospered in Mozambique. Alvarenga died in Angola. The priests went to convents.
paths.cap6.scenes.8.title: April 21, 1792
paths.cap6.scenes.8.lines.0.text: Largo da Lampadosa, Rio de Janeiro. Today, Praça Tiradentes.
paths.cap6.scenes.8.lines.1.text: Tiradentes is hanged and quartered. His body is displayed along the New Road; his house razed and salted.
paths.cap6.scenes.8.lines.2.text: Declared infamous for generations. Today, April 21 is a national holiday.
paths.cap6.scenes.9.title: 1889 · The beard
paths.cap6.scenes.9.lines.1.text: Invented by the Republic, a hundred years later. Ensigns didn't wear beards, and prisoners had shaved heads.
paths.cap6.scenes.9.lines.3.text: 1889: the Town of São José becomes Tiradentes. Irony: Maria I, who upheld the sentence, was Prince José's daughter.
paths.cap6.scenes.10.title: The bell rings
paths.cap6.scenes.10.intro: Last quiz of Phase 1. Get 2 out of 3.
paths.cap6.scenes.11.title: Back to the Lookout
paths.cap6.scenes.11.egg.label: ⛲ Drink from the fountain with the empty canteen
paths.cap6.scenes.11.egg.lines.0.text: Buck goes back to the fountain, fills the canteen and drinks. The sky spins again…
paths.cap6.scenes.11.lines.2.text: Here the bell talks. Now you know how to listen.
paths.cap6.scenes.12.title: END OF PHASE 1
paths.cap6.scenes.12.text: 300 years, from brazilwood to the gallows. Next stop: Phase 2 · Rio, Petrópolis and the Empire.
paths.quests.QST-01.title: Who got there first?
paths.quests.QST-01.brief: A captain swears he saw Brazil's coast before Cabral. Find out who it was and when.
paths.quests.QST-01.witnesses.0.text: He was captain of the Niña, on Columbus's voyage.
paths.quests.QST-01.witnesses.1.text: He arrived one January, before the 13-ship fleet.
paths.quests.QST-01.witnesses.2.text: By the treaty, that land was Portugal's. That's why Spain didn't even claim it.
paths.quests.QST-01.suspects.1.why: Cabral arrived in April. Someone got there earlier.
paths.quests.QST-01.suspects.2.name: Christopher Columbus
paths.quests.QST-01.suspects.2.why: Columbus reached the Bahamas, not Brazil.
paths.quests.QST-01.suspects.3.name: Amerigo Vespucci
paths.quests.QST-02.title: The red shipment vanished
paths.quests.QST-02.brief: Brazilwood logs vanished from the trading post before the leaseholder's ship arrived. Who took them?
paths.quests.QST-02.witnesses.0.text: The post stored the logs until the next ship. There were about 24 of us.
paths.quests.QST-02.witnesses.1.text: The red dye was worth a lot in Europe. Plenty of people wanted a piece without paying the leaseholder.
paths.quests.QST-02.witnesses.2.text: The ship that took the logs didn't have Portugal's cross on its sails.
paths.quests.QST-02.suspects.0.name: A French smuggler
paths.quests.QST-02.suspects.1.why: Noronha was the leaseholder: the logs were already his.
paths.quests.QST-02.suspects.2.name: The neighboring village
paths.quests.QST-02.suspects.2.why: The Indigenous people were the ones cutting the logs, through barter. They didn't need to steal their own work.
paths.quests.QST-02.suspects.3.name: A Spanish captain
paths.quests.QST-03.title: From Recife to New York
paths.quests.QST-03.brief: When the Dutch left Recife, a group carried the city's story north. Who were they, and when did they arrive?
paths.quests.QST-03.witnesses.0.text: Recife had canals, bridges and the first synagogue in the Americas.
paths.quests.QST-03.witnesses.1.text: After the battles, the Dutch surrendered.
paths.quests.QST-03.witnesses.2.text: Some went to the Caribbean. Others reached New Amsterdam, the future New York.
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.0.name: 23 Jewish refugees from Recife
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.1.name: Maurice of Nassau
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.1.why: Nassau left Brazil in 1644, before the surrender.
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.2.name: The painters Frans Post and Eckhout
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.2.why: They painted Dutch Brazil, but founded nothing in New York.
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.3.name: The West India Company
paths.quests.QST-03.suspects.3.why: The WIC took Salvador and Pernambuco. It was people who reached New Amsterdam.
paths.quests.QST-04.title: Who stole the fifth of 1720?
paths.quests.QST-04.brief: In 1720 Vila Rica caught fire and a fifth of everyone's gold vanished. Issue the Devassa.
paths.quests.QST-04.witnesses.0.text: He talked about bars with the king's seal. No more gold dust, ever.
paths.quests.QST-04.witnesses.1.text: I saw a hill on fire in Vila Rica. The ones who ordered it burned were government men.
paths.quests.QST-04.witnesses.2.text: Folks were hiding gold inside hollow wooden saints… or so they say.
paths.quests.QST-04.suspects.0.name: The Fifth Collector
paths.quests.QST-04.suspects.1.why: Filipe led the revolt against the tax and was hanged. He didn't steal the fifth: the fifth was taken from him.
paths.quests.QST-04.suspects.2.why: Pascoal was a rich man revolting against the tax. He was sent to Portugal.
paths.quests.QST-04.suspects.3.name: The Count of Assumar
paths.quests.QST-04.suspects.3.why: Warm! Assumar worked for him. But what takes the fifth isn't a person.
paths.quests.QST-05.title: The book the king doesn't want you to read
paths.quests.QST-05.brief: A book described the mines and the gold roads. The Crown had it seized. Who wrote it?
paths.quests.QST-05.witnesses.0.text: The author was a Jesuit. He wrote too much.
paths.quests.QST-05.witnesses.1.text: The “hell, purgatory and paradise” line is his.
paths.quests.QST-05.witnesses.2.text: In Brazil you couldn't even print: presses were banned until 1808.
paths.quests.QST-05.suspects.1.why: Fernão Dias was a bandeirante, not a writer.
paths.quests.QST-05.suspects.2.why: Nunes Viana led the emboabas; he didn't write a book.
paths.quests.QST-05.suspects.3.why: Borba Gato traded gold for a pardon. Not books.
paths.quests.QST-06.title: The emerald that wasn't
paths.quests.QST-06.brief: An emerald hunter died happy with his treasure. Who was he, and what did he really have?
paths.quests.QST-06.witnesses.0.text: He spent 7 years in the backlands.
paths.quests.QST-06.witnesses.1.text: His trails and farm plots became the road of the gold rush.
paths.quests.QST-06.witnesses.2.text: I found gold on the Rio das Velhas… in exchange for a pardon. But that's another story.
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.0.name: Fernão Dias (they were tourmalines)
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.1.name: Borba Gato (they were diamonds)
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.1.why: Borba Gato found gold, and diamonds only appeared in 1729.
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.2.name: Arzão (it was quartz)
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.2.why: Arzão brought the first gold samples, in 1693.
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.3.name: Antônio Dias (it was black gold)
paths.quests.QST-06.suspects.3.why: Antônio Dias found real gold, in 1698.
paths.quests.QST-07.title: Who gave up the conspirators?
paths.quests.QST-07.brief: The plan was waiting for the derrama. The derrama was called off and everyone was arrested. Someone talked. Who, and when?
paths.quests.QST-07.witnesses.0.text: They wanted a republic, a university and São João del-Rei as the capital.
paths.quests.QST-07.witnesses.1.text: One of them owed the Crown a fortune.
paths.quests.QST-07.witnesses.2.text: Afterwards, the informer got his debts forgiven. A plea bargain in the 18th century.
paths.quests.QST-07.suspects.1.name: Father Toledo
paths.quests.QST-07.suspects.1.why: Father Toledo threw the party. He was part of the group, not the informer.
paths.quests.QST-07.suspects.2.why: Tiradentes was the only one who admitted everything. He gave up no one.
paths.quests.QST-07.suspects.3.why: Cláudio was arrested and found dead in his cell.
paths.quests.QST-08.title: The letter to Jefferson
paths.quests.QST-08.brief: Two years before the conspiracy, someone asked the United States for help. Who was it?
paths.quests.QST-08.witnesses.1.text: The US minister to France received him. He was cordial.
paths.quests.QST-08.witnesses.2.text: A promise? None. Jefferson ghosted Brazil.
paths.quests.QST-08.suspects.1.why: Tiradentes patrolled the New Road. He never went to France.
paths.quests.QST-08.suspects.2.why: Gonzaga ended up exiled in Mozambique.
paths.quests.QST-08.suspects.3.why: Alvarenga was the father at the 1788 baptism.
paths.quests.QST-09.title: Tiradentes' beard
paths.quests.QST-09.brief: The Tiradentes of the statues has a saint's beard. But ensigns didn't wear beards. Who invented it?
paths.quests.QST-09.witnesses.0.text: Ensigns wore a mustache, at most.
paths.quests.QST-09.witnesses.2.text: A hundred years later, someone needed a hero who looked like Christ.
paths.quests.QST-09.suspects.0.name: The Republic
paths.quests.QST-09.suspects.1.name: Queen Maria I
paths.quests.QST-09.suspects.1.why: Maria I upheld the sentence. She had no wish to make a hero.
paths.quests.QST-09.suspects.2.name: The conspirators themselves
paths.quests.QST-09.suspects.2.why: They never even got to start the revolt.
paths.quests.QST-10.title: Why does the river have that name?
paths.quests.QST-10.brief: They say the Rio das Mortes, River of the Dead, got its name from the Capão of Betrayal. Did it?
paths.quests.QST-10.witnesses.0.text: In 1709 we surrendered under a promise of life, and they broke it.
paths.quests.QST-10.witnesses.1.text: I heard that name before the war. Lots of people drowned at the crossings.
paths.quests.QST-10.witnesses.2.text: The war only reinforced the legend.
paths.quests.QST-10.suspects.0.name: An older name: crossings and fights
paths.quests.QST-10.suspects.1.name: The bodies of the Capão of Betrayal
paths.quests.QST-10.suspects.1.why: That's the legend. The name appears before the war.
paths.quests.QST-10.suspects.2.name: An order from the king
paths.quests.QST-10.suspects.2.why: The king named towns, not this river.
paths.quests.QST-10.suspects.3.name: The emboabas, to scare people

paths.colony.buildings.1.desc: Food. Whoever only mines goes hungry (C31).

paths.colony.buildings.5.desc: After 1720, without it the Fifth becomes 30% (fine for gold dust).

paths.colony.buildings.7.desc: Prestige. And the town splits into brotherhoods (C48).

paths.colony.events.0.text: Portugal founds its first town. Now you can build yours (council + pillory + church).
paths.colony.events.1.title: Who worked the sugar mills
paths.colony.events.1.text: In real history, the sugar mills ran on enslaved labor: first Indigenous, then African. Brazil received about 4.8 million enslaved Africans. The game does not turn people into a resource.
paths.colony.events.2.title: Iberian Union
paths.colony.events.2.text: Spain inherits Portugal, and Spain's enemies start attacking Brazil.
paths.colony.events.3.title: Pirates!
paths.colony.events.3.text: Thomas Cavendish sacks Santos. You lose part of your sugar.
paths.colony.events.4.title: The Dutch
paths.colony.events.4.text: The WIC takes Pernambuco, the heart of sugar.
paths.colony.events.5.title: Sugar crisis
paths.colony.events.5.text: Antilles sugar is cheaper. From now on, each sugar mill yields half. Go inland!
paths.colony.events.6.title: GOLD!
paths.colony.events.6.text: Gold appears in Minas. Do the Age Up to build gold diggings.
paths.colony.events.7.title: Hunger in the mines
paths.colony.events.7.text: Nobody farmed. Without farm plots, the population drops.
paths.colony.events.8.title: Emboaba War
paths.colony.events.8.text: Paulistas against outsiders. You lose a few people.
paths.colony.events.9.title: Smelting Houses
paths.colony.events.9.text: Gold dust banned: all melted, stamped and taxed a fifth. Revolt in Vila Rica; Filipe dos Santos is hanged.
paths.colony.events.10.title: Capitation
paths.colony.events.10.text: A head tax: every person pays 1 gold.
paths.colony.events.11.title: The 100 arrobas
paths.colony.events.11.text: The capitation, too heavy, is dropped. Instead, the Crown demands a Fifth quota per decade. Short? It becomes debt.
paths.colony.events.12.title: Surface gold runs out
paths.colony.events.12.text: Easy to find, easy to run out: every digging yields less.
paths.colony.events.13.title: The capital comes down the mountain
paths.colony.events.13.text: Brazil's capital moves to Rio. The Estrada Real carries the gold there.
paths.colony.events.14.title: The 1785 decree
paths.colony.events.14.text: The queen bans textile manufacturing. Your weaving shops are closed.
paths.colony.events.15.title: The derrama called off
paths.colony.events.15.text: The derrama was coming. Silvério betrays the Conspiracy; Barbacena calls it off and arrests everyone.
paths.cap4.scenes.7.egg.label: 🗺️ Crossed-out map
paths.cap4.scenes.7.egg.lines.0.text: A 1711 map on the governor’s desk: “Vila Rica de A̶l̶b̶u̶q̶u̶e̶r̶q̶u̶e̶”.
paths.cap4.scenes.7.egg.lines.1.text: Governor Antônio de Albuquerque named the town after himself. The king had it crossed out.
paths.cap5.scenes.0.egg.label: 👁️ Count the faces
paths.cap5.scenes.0.egg.lines.0.text: In the Matriz, an estípite column has carved faces. Count them: girl, young woman, woman, old woman.
paths.cap5.scenes.0.egg.lines.1.text: The four ages of woman on one column. Everything passes, except the waiting list to marry in the Matriz.
paths.cap6.scenes.4.title: 1787 · France
paths.cap5.scenes.7.end.2.text: And in 1763 the capital moves from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro. Follow the money, literally.
